newsitem.title: USA: Dole presses attack on Clinton's trustworthiness.
newsitem.headline: Dole presses attack on Clinton's trustworthiness.

text.p: Republican candidate Bob Dole asked voters on Sunday to look at him and President Bill Clinton and then vote for the one they would be proud to have in the White House.

With some polls showing Americans think Dole is more trustworthy than his Democratic rival, Dole told a New Jersey rally: "I want you to be proud of the vote you cast. I want you to take a look at Bob Dole. Take a look at Bill Clinton ... which one do you want in the White House?
"Cast your vote with pride," he said.

Campaigning by bus across a state that is considered vital if he is to win a come-from-behind victory, Dole said Clinton used scare tactics and fear to distort Dole's economic plans and their effect on senior citizens and veterans.
"For Bill Clinton every day is Halloween," Dole told supporters at a rally in Somerville, New Jersey.
"My biggest fear is that if he gets re-elected to another four years, you better hold on to your wallets and everything that isn't nailed down, because he's coming at you," Dole said.
He stressed his proposed 15 percent tax cut in a state where the popular Republican Gov. Christine Todd Whitman has lowered taxes.
Dole has been attacking Clinton for being unreliable, untrustworthy and a man who does not keep his promises.
"We're going to say what we mean, we're going to keep our word," said Dole.

"It's not over til it's over," Dole told a largely Italian-American crowd at a Columbus Day Parade in Newark, N.J., quoting baseball legend Yogi Berra and joking that Berra was one of his campaign advisers.
Dole travelled by bus through New Jersey, where a similar tour last week was cut short by the remnants of tropical storm Josephine.
A state of swing voters, New Jersey has 15 electoral votes, a popular Republican governor and a history of voting for Republicans for president -- although it backed Clinton in 1992.

Dole lags well behind Clinton in public opinion surveys but his aides and allies, as well as other prominent Republicans like House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, have ratcheted up their attacks on Clinton, using language far harsher than Dole himself has chosen.
Dole's campaign has been riven by internal battles, which have spilled into the open, over how hard to hit Clinton on character and ethics.

While his advisers battle it out -- thereby dragging all the character accusations into the public eye -- Dole has walked a fine line between raising questions about Clinton's reliability and trustworthiness while not getting into Clinton's private life or dwelling on the Whitewater scandal.
